translationRepairs: Hanzhi marched on Jin and Jiang. Quanyi struck and seized Heyang. Hanzhi ran to Li Keyong; Jin sent help and penned Quanyi tight.
Hanzhi marched against Jin and Jiang Prefectures. Quanyi struck behind him and seized Heyang. Hanzhi fled to Jin, whose troops came to his aid and pressed Quanyi hard in siege.
The first 晉 and 絳 are Jin and Jiang Prefectures, while 罕之奔晉 refers to the Jin polity. The revision distinguishes them and removes Li Keyong, whom this sentence does not name.
Tang ended; he served Liang and asked for a new name. The Founder called him Zongyi.
Tang ended; he served Liang and asked for a new name. The Founder called him Zongshi.
宗奭 is pronounced Zongshi. Zongyi misreads 奭 as 義 and conflicts with the extraction's correctly romanized Chinese name.
Defeated at Gaoxian, Zhu Wen sickened on the march home. He summered at Quanyi’s Festival Garden ten days and forced Quanyi’s wife and daughters.

After his army was defeated at Tiao County, Zhu Wen fell ill on the road back to Luoyang. He spent ten days escaping the summer heat at Quanyi's Festival Garden, where he forced Quanyi's wife and daughters to submit to him.
The place is 蓨縣, conventionally Tiao County, not Gaoxian. The revision also completes the English sense of 皆迫淫之 instead of leaving 'forced' without stating what the women were forced to do.
His wife Lady Chu was quick and had a tongue like a blade. She went straight in and snapped: “Zongyi? A dirt farmer, nothing more!
His wife Lady Chu was quick and had a tongue like a blade. She went straight in and snapped: “Zongshi? A dirt farmer, nothing more!
Lady Chu addresses Zhang Quanyi by the Liang-bestowed name 宗奭, which is Zongshi, not Zongyi.
Zhu Youqian, styled Deguang, came from Xuzhou.
Zhu Youqian, styled Deguang, came from Xu Prefecture.
許州 is Xu Prefecture, centered on modern Xuchang, and is distinct from Xuzhou 徐州. The replacement corrects the mistaken place name.
Li Keyong came out of Ze and Lu, met Huaiying at Jie, broke him utterly, chased to Baijing Ridge, burned torches into him at night, broke him again, and Liang pulled off.

The Prince of Jin came from Ze and Lu to rescue him. He met Huaiying at Jie County and routed him, pursued him to Baijing Ridge, and attacked by torchlight at night. Huaiying was defeated again, and the Liang army withdrew.

The Chinese names the Prince of Jin, not Li Keyong, who had died in 908. The parallel Jiu Wudai Shi account says Youqian appealed to Zhuangzong for this rescue; the revision also replaces the unidiomatic phrase 'burned torches into him.'
Youqian slept drunk in Li Keyong’s tent. The Prince looked him over and told his men: “All that honor—and such short arms!”
Youqian fell asleep drunk in the Prince of Jin's tent. The prince looked him over and said to his attendants, 'The Prince of Ji may be very exalted, but unfortunately his arms are short!'
This is the same Prince of Jin as in s0069, not Li Keyong. The revision restores the full force of the quoted assessment rather than compressing it into an unexplained fragment.
Edict: Jiji kill Lingde at Suizhou; Wang Sitong kill Lingxi at Xuzhou; Xia Luqi wipe out the clan at Hezhong.
An edict ordered Jiji, Prince of Wei, to kill Lingde at Suizhou, Wang Sitong to kill Lingxi at Xu Prefecture, and Xia Luqi to exterminate the rest of the family at Hezhong.
許州 is Xu Prefecture rather than Xuzhou 徐州. The revision also restores Jiji's title and turns the telegraphic proposal into grammatical English while preserving all three commands.
Lu Siduo came from Linhuang in Cao.
Lu Siduo was from Linhuang in Chan Prefecture.
澶州 is Chan Prefecture, not Cao Prefecture 曹州. The revision restores both the correct administrative name and natural biographical English.
Hanzhi led troops to attack Jin and Jiang; Quanyi raided and took Heyang; Hanzhi fled to Jin; Jin sent troops to aid Hanzhi and besieged Quanyi very hard.
Hanzhi led troops to attack Jin Prefecture and Jiang Prefecture; Quanyi seized Heyang in a surprise attack; Hanzhi fled to Jin, which sent troops to aid him and press Quanyi hard in siege.
The literal field had the same unresolved collision between Jin Prefecture and the Jin polity as the reviewed idiomatic field; this paired correction distinguishes them.
When Tang fell, Quanyi served Liang and again asked to change his name; the Founder bestowed the name Zongyi.
When Tang fell, Quanyi served Liang and again asked to change his name; the Founder bestowed the name Zongshi.
The literal field repeated the same misreading of 宗奭 as Zongyi; Zongshi is the correct romanization.

When the Founder’s army was defeated at Gaoxian he fell ill on the road, returned to Luoyang, visited Quanyi’s Festival Garden to escape the heat, and stayed ten days; Quanyi’s wife and daughters were all forced to his bed.

When the Founder’s army was defeated at Tiao County, he fell ill on the road and returned to Luoyang. He visited Quanyi’s Festival Garden to escape the summer heat and stayed ten days; Quanyi’s wife and daughters were all forced to submit to him.
The literal field repeated Gaoxian for 蓨縣 and needed the same Tiao County correction, with the coercion expressed without the euphemistic and unsupported phrase 'to his bed.'
Quanyi’s wife, Lady Chu, was clever and sharp-tongued; she rushed in to see him and said in a fierce voice: “Zongyi is nothing but an old farmer!
Quanyi’s wife, Lady Chu, was clever and sharp-tongued; she rushed in to see him and said in a fierce voice: “Zongshi is nothing but an old farmer!
The literal quotation repeated the same incorrect romanization of 宗奭 and is corrected in parallel with the reviewed idiomatic field.
Zhu Youqian, courtesy name Deguang, was a native of Xuzhou.
Zhu Youqian, courtesy name Deguang, was a native of Xu Prefecture.
The literal field likewise confused 許州 with Xuzhou 徐州; the paired correction restores Xu Prefecture.
An edict ordered Prince Jiji to kill Lingde at Suizhou, Wang Sitong to kill Lingxi at Xuzhou, and Xia Luqi to exterminate his household at Hezhong.
An edict ordered Jiji, Prince of Wei, to kill Lingde at Suizhou, Wang Sitong to kill Lingxi at Xu Prefecture, and Xia Luqi to exterminate his household at Hezhong.
The literal field repeated the 許州/Xuzhou confusion and reversed the natural order of Jiji's name and title; this paired correction fixes both.
Lu Siduo was a man of Linhuang in Cao.
Lu Siduo was a native of Linhuang in Chan Prefecture.
The literal field likewise misread 澶州 as Cao; the paired correction restores Chan Prefecture and the standard biographical formula.
